section.title: Build tooling around real pain, then earn adoption
section.deck: The Bento story links a staff-level technical vision with onboarding, legacy support, team creation, and explicitly agreed exploration.

blocks.question: What was the work behind your senior-staff-equivalent promotion?
answer: The guest began on a project estimating usage of a Facebook property around 2015. Moving between separate data-pipeline and machine-learning systems was cumbersome, so he built helper scripts that let pipeline work live within the orchestration environment. Sensible defaults removed repeated boilerplate, with an escape hatch for advanced configuration. He estimates that a task needing roughly 300 lines in the older system could need about 20 in his library.

That experience redirected his interest from a single analysis to helping analysts and machine-learning engineers work faster. Notebook setup was another repeated pain: people used outdated wikis to install Jupyter or RStudio manually. With his manager’s agreement, he spent an initial two or three months exploring an automated setup, then recruited others. The earliest Bento was just a setup script; the larger vision was a browser-accessible environment integrated with internal libraries and eventually other languages.

Over roughly a year, the team built the platform and on-demand instances that users could request and release without maintaining their own server. He also assembled a team of six to eight people by inviting engineers who already loved building tools on the side to do it full time. He moved into a tech-lead-manager role and says his TLM2 promotion depended largely on his individual technical work and the Bento vision. The host explains that level as senior-manager or senior-staff equivalent.
blocks.speaker: Guest

blocks.question: How did you turn a useful internal tool into something widely adopted?
answer: Bento did not initially require converting everybody’s existing workflow. The team targeted onboarding programs, where new data users had no attachment to legacy setup. In a fast-growing company, that supplied many users; existing employees then saw more colleagues on the new system.

For people who remained on legacy notebooks, the team provided maintenance and support in previously underserved channels. That created trust before a migration request. When someone needed an awkward setup, the team could offer either a long manual recipe or the simpler supported Bento path.

The team also spoke with analytics leaders about concrete pain in their groups. Those conversations revealed a larger backlog of data-tooling needs. Because no dedicated team served that area, the guest moved from core data science into developer infrastructure to create one. Adoption was therefore a mix of a convenient entry point, service to existing users, leadership relationships, and a fitting organizational home.

blocks.question: How do you take a promising risk when short-term performance expectations are strict?
answer: The guest thinks underperformance has greater consequences than it did a decade earlier, but the key practice is the same: agree on expectations before departing from normal work. He was assigned to data consulting, while the proposed work was infrastructure, so he asked his manager and skip to make a bounded exploration part of his job.

If the tool succeeded, the team benefited; if it failed, completing an agreed exploration was still the expectation. He sees that as much safer than disappearing for three months and returning with work nobody knew had displaced his normal obligations.

Over-communicate and be prepared to hear no. He credits a manager who supported this experiment and remembers later proposals that leadership rejected. The story does not promise that every risk can be negotiated away or that an exploratory project guarantees a promotion.
